one_liner: About 1,200-line C virtual machine for an x86-style assembly language; a hand-written fib(34) ran about 1.7x faster than PUC Lua in 2015.
what_it_does: TinyVM loads a text file of x86-flavoured assembly (17 32-bit registers, labels, push/pop/call/ret, cmp and conditional jumps, %include/%define preprocessor), parses it into bytecode and runs it. The C API is four calls: tvm_vm_create(), tvm_vm_interpret(vm, filename), tvm_vm_run(vm), tvm_vm_destroy(vm); results are read back from vm->mem registers or memory, and the only output instruction is prn (print an integer). There is no high-level language, no host-function interface and no way to load a program from a string, so it is not a drop-in for Lua.
how_it_is_fast: All decoding happens once at load time: each line becomes an int opcode plus an array of int* operand pointers (registers point into the register file, immediates and label targets point to heap-allocated ints, [n] memory operands point straight into a 64 MB arena), and labels are resolved to instruction indices through a hash table. The run loop is a plain switch in tvm_step on 32-bit ints with no type tags, boxing, bounds checks or garbage collector. The benchmark program itself is hand-written assembly that sums leaf values into a register (ebx) instead of returning values, so each fib call is only a handful of trivial instructions.
when_to_use: Studying or teaching interpreter construction: the whole VM (lexer, preprocessor, parser, dispatch loop) is about 1,200 lines of dependency-free C under MIT.
A back end for a toy compiler or code generator that can emit x86-like assembly text and wants to run it portably without native code generation.
Integer-only kernels on hosts with only a C compiler, including freestanding builds linked against the mlibc submodule.
A minimal baseline when measuring dispatch overhead of other VM designs.
when_not_to_use: You need an embedded scripting language: there are no strings, floats, tables, closures or GC, and scripts are assembly listings.

Running untrusted programs: memory operands, stack pushes and jump targets are not bounds-checked, and div/mod by zero or signed overflow are C undefined behaviour, so a bad program can crash or corrupt the host.
The host must expose functions to scripts or feed programs from memory: the TODO file lists 'C interface' and 'JIT compilation' as not done, and tvm_vm_interpret only accepts a file name.
You need a maintained project: last commit 2018-03-22, the TODO says the debugger 'doesn't work', and issue #41 (parser error handling) is open without a reply.
Memory-tight hosts: every tvm_vm_create callocs a fixed 64 MB address space (MIN_MEMORY_SIZE) with a 2 MB stack inside it, not configurable through the API.

integration.form: static lib (libtvm.a) plus the tvmi command-line runner, or source-drop of libtvm/*.c and include/tvm
integration.dependencies: none beyond the C standard library; optional mlibc git submodule for freestanding builds
integration.min_toolchain: C99-level compiler; the GNUmakefile builds with clang -std=gnu11 -O3 -pedantic -Werror, and Scriptorium built its 2015 snapshot with MSVC 2013/2015
integration.platforms: any platform with a C compiler (no architecture-specific code); the README documents only UNIX-like builds with make
integration.thread_safety: not documented; all VM state lives in struct tvm_ctx and libtvm has no mutable globals (only const opcode and register name tables), but prn writes through printf

gotchas: Harness flaw: TinyVM was never timed in the same batch as Lua. Its five averages (0.786-0.815 s) are in a later block of bench.csv (lines 93-96 and 105) that has no Lua row, while the 1.341 s Lua figure comes from an earlier batch (line 65); Lua's other batch was 2.359 s. Duktape, timed in both blocks (9.544 s vs 9.06-9.71 s), suggests the machine ran at similar speed, so 1.7x is plausible but cross-batch. The Lua row runs a bare 'lua' from PATH (the repo has no lua.exe; lua/ holds only lua-5.3.1 and luajit-2.0 sources), so its version and build are unrecorded.

Not like-for-like: fib.tvm is hand-written assembly that accumulates leaf values in ebx with no return values or frames, while fib.lua returns values and looks up the global fibR in _ENV on every call. bench.cc never checks output; fib(34) is 5702887 (the 433494437 in the fib.lua comment and in the record's workload is fib(43)), and fib.tvm's logic does yield 5702887.

Record correction: Scriptorium's tinyvm/make.bat does state the flags, cl /Ox /Oy /MT /DNDEBUG. The timed code is a 2015 snapshot with the older API (tvm_create, tvm_interpret, tvm_run); HEAD renamed these to tvm_vm_* and the runner to tvmi, with the same switch dispatch in tvm_step.

[n] operands are turned into raw pointers into the 64 MB arena at parse time (value from strtoul, cast to int) with no range check, and jmp/call through a register set the instruction index to any value, so out-of-range addresses or jumps read or write outside VM memory.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TinyVM only as an assembly-level teaching or codegen-target VM; for embedded scripting, Pawn (a compiled C-like language with host natives; 0.719 s C core, 0.384 s asm core in the same table) or Lua/Luau give a real language and host interface, and c4-jit (0.136 s) is far faster on the same fib(34) test.
verified_claims_summary: r-lyeh's Scriptorium (2015, MSVC 2013/2015 with /Ox /Oy /MT /DNDEBUG per tinyvm/make.bat, AMD A10 3.8 GHz, Windows 7 64-bit) timed whole-process runs of the 2015 TinyVM on a hand-written fib(34) assembly program: best 5-run average 0.786 s against 1.341 s for an unidentified PUC Lua on PATH timed in an earlier batch, about 1.7x (derived from page data); against Lua's other recorded batch (2.359 s) the ratio would be 3.0x.
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-03-22 (last commits were scan-build and memory-leak fixes) but MIT-licensed, dependency-free and small enough to vendor; treat it as a teaching VM rather than a production scripting engine.
